note: First-pass dataset. Rarity tiers and regional ranges need review by a Kruger guide before launch — see docs/SPEC.md.

species.description: Pig-like body, tubular snout, donkey ears, an arched back and a thick tail — but you'll almost never see one. Strictly nocturnal, and even a night drive turns one up perhaps once in a hundred outings. Uses 20cm digging claws to break open termite mounds, then laps up the workers with a long sticky tongue. Its burrows go on to shelter dozens of other species — porcupines, warthogs, snakes, even wild dogs — long after the aardvark itself has moved on. A confirmed sighting is a proper trophy.
species.habitat: Woodland and grassland with termite mounds
species.bestTimeToSpot: Late on a night drive, well after dark

population.note: Not counted. Widespread across the park and almost never seen, so no survey has ever put a number on it.

species.description: Small striped hyena on stilt-thin legs, mane raised along the spine when alarmed — a nervous, slinking silhouette in torchlight. Not a hunter: laps up around 200,000 harvester termites in a single night with a broad sticky tongue, using dozens of small non-functional teeth that barely chew. Very rarely seen, and easily mistaken for a striped hyena at first glance until you notice the size and slender build. Night drives on open grassland at the edges of the mopaneveld give the realistic chance.

Nocturnal — you won't see one by day. Dog-sized, hunched shoulders and a low-slung walk, coat densely spotted black on cream with a black bandit mask across the eyes. Trots along roads and firebreaks at night with the head lowered, following scent trails, and marks territory by dragging a musky gland along low branches. Historically the source of civet musk used in European perfumery. Night drives out of Olifants, Skukuza and Berg-en-Dal give the realistic chance; almost never turns up on a self-drive.

Grey giants with fan-shaped ears and long tusks, moving in matriarchal herds with calves kept in the middle. Kruger holds close to 30,000 — one of the densest populations in Africa — and they browse over 100 tree species, sometimes tearing down whole marulas in a single session. Give a bull space if he fans his ears, shakes his head, or splashes dust: those are the warnings before a real charge. Trunks contain roughly 40,000 muscle bundles, enough control to pick up a marula seed or push over a tree.
species.habitat: Everywhere, concentrating near rivers in the dry season

species.description: Blotched brown, black and white coats — no two dogs alike, and each pack member is genuinely identifiable by pattern. Huge round Mickey-Mouse ears and constant high-pitched twittering when the pack is on the move. Around 250 left in Kruger and listed Endangered globally. Packs sprint after impala or kudu in a moving swarm, then collapse in a heap on the cool tar to digest. Kruger's stronghold is the central and northern sections around Letaba and Mopani. Never follow at high speed — vehicles are a leading cause of pack deaths.

Looks like a lean tabby with longer legs, but the rich rufous behind the ears is the field-guide diagnostic. Almost always nocturnal, though the resident individual around Satara Rest Camp is the easiest bet, hunting rodents along the perimeter fence at last light. Direct ancestor of every domestic cat on earth — all descended from a small population that entered Middle Eastern grain stores about 10,000 years ago. Interbreeds readily with feral cats, and genuinely pure wild ones are getting harder to find in Kruger.

Troops of 15 to 30 charging across the road nose-to-tail, dark bands running crossways over a grizzled brown back. Constant high-pitched twittering as they forage, and every adult watches out for the others' pups — one of the most cooperative mammals in Africa. Common throughout the park, often around Skukuza and Berg-en-Dal camps, where they investigate camp bins and rustle noisily through leaf litter. Sleep at night stuffed into disused termitaria, moving den every few days as the food thins out around each one.

Silver-grey body, black face-mask, huge disc-like ears — small enough to fit in a hat, and permanently listening for underground insects. Very rare in Kruger; the stronghold is further west in the Kalahari, and here you'll only occasionally turn one up on the central basalt plains around Satara. Lowers the ears to the ground to pinpoint termite and beetle-larva movement, then digs straight down. Family groups of parents and pups forage together, and unusually for a canid the male does most of the pup-rearing.

Hook-lipped browser standing in thick bush rather than on the open plains — smaller than a White Rhino, ears rotating alertly, notoriously bad-tempered. Just a couple of hundred left in Kruger after the poaching crisis of the 2010s halved the population. If a black rhino charges the car, stay in the vehicle and let it hit — most 'charges' are bluffs, and the animal cannot see well enough to press one home against a stationary target. Northern and central Kruger give the best odds, especially in mopane thickets.

population.note: SANParks stopped publishing rhino numbers so that poachers cannot use them. Kruger holds one of the last significant populations left anywhere.

species.description: Fox-sized canid with russet flanks and a distinctive black saddle streaked silver — the saddle is the giveaway against the plainer Side-striped Jackal. Trots along alone or in pairs at dawn and dusk, hunting rodents, hares and birds; also scavenges around lion kills, snatching scraps as the lions doze off. Yipping howls carry across the veld at night, often triggering a chain response from other pairs. Common throughout Kruger's open country, especially the central plains around Satara and Nsemani Dam.

Dark grey with a shaggy dark beard and forward-hooked horns, usually mixed in with zebra herds on the open plains — the wildebeest sees, the zebra hears, and neither wants to be at the edge of the mixed group when lions are close. Central grasslands from Satara to Orpen are the Kruger stronghold. Nasal snorting calls carry a surprising distance in the still morning air. Calves are born a rusty tan and turn grey after about two months. Not part of the great Serengeti-Mara migration; Kruger's wildebeest are residents.

Shaggier and darker than a Spotted Hyena, with a long mane over the shoulders and pointed ears — the coat is the field-guide diagnostic. Extremely rare in Kruger; mostly restricted to the far north, and scavenges alone at night rather than hunting in clans. A daylight sighting anywhere in the park is almost unheard of. Ranges over huge distances each night — 30km is a normal walk — and marks territory with a milky paste from the anal gland pressed onto grass stems, a signal system that lasts weeks.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Deep night, far north — essentially chance

species.description: Chestnut-brown antelope with faint white spots and stripes down the flanks; only the male carries the straight spiral horns. Solitary and shy in dense riverine bush — the Letaba and Sabie forests are the easiest spots, and Letaba Rest Camp has habituated individuals that will feed within a few metres of the boardwalks. Bounds off with a sharp dog-like bark that surprises first-time visitors. Excellent swimmers, and will cross the Olifants River in flood if pushed.

Rarely seen from a car — nocturnal and secretive along dense riverine bush and thickets. Reddish-brown pig with a pale erect mane down the spine and pointed ear tufts, quite unlike the warthog's tail-flagging profile. Any pig you see in daylight in open country is a warthog, not this. Bushpigs move in family groups called sounders, root deep for tubers and bulbs, and occasionally raid crops outside the park boundary. Night drives out of Skukuza and Lower Sabie give the realistic chance.

Massive black bulk, sweeping horns fused across the forehead into a heavy boss on the bulls — the boss thickens with age and is what trophy hunters used to prize. Herds of several hundred churn the ground at waterholes and river crossings. Around 40,000 in the park. Solitary or small-group 'dagga boys' — old bulls kicked out of the breeding herd, plastered in dry mud — are unpredictable and cause more human injuries than lions. Give any lone bull wide berth, and never get out on foot.
species.habitat: Grassland and woodland near permanent water

species.description: Almost never seen by day. Rustling at night around rest camps, quills clattering against fence posts — black-and-white banded quills up to 30cm long. Africa's largest rodent, and the largest of any porcupine species anywhere. Try Skukuza, Olifants and Berg-en-Dal after dark, or a formal night drive. Contrary to legend, quills do not fire; they detach on contact when the porcupine backs into a threat, driving them deep. A lion or leopard that gets a face full of quills often dies days later from the septic wounds.
species.habitat: Widespread; shelters in caves and burrows

species.description: Rufous cat with long pointed black ear tufts, powerful hindquarters and no spots — nothing else in Kruger looks like one. Nocturnal and shy; most people who see one get a single second of it in a night-drive spotlight. Can leap over 3m to swat a bird from mid-air, and takes prey up to the size of a young impala. The Afrikaans name 'rooikat' simply means red cat. Try quiet gravel roads in the central section at first light, or arrange a night drive from Satara.

Big dog-faced primate in troops of 30 to 100, walking on all fours along the roadside and picnic-site verges. The 'wah-hoo!' alarm bark from a sentinel male warns of a leopard nearby — worth listening for, then scanning the treeline. Keep vehicle windows shut and never leave food visible: they will open unlocked doors, and troops around Skukuza and Lower Sabie have learned exactly which car models to try. Long adolescence and dominance politics that would exhaust a soap opera; some troops have been studied continuously for over fifty years.
species.habitat: Everywhere, especially near camps and koppies
species.bestTimeToSpot: Daylight — roosts in trees at night

species.description: Slim, small-headed cat with black tear-lines running from eye down the cheek, and simple spots — not the leopard's dark rosettes. Usually on open plains, often perched on a termite mound or road verge scanning for impala. About 150 in Kruger, most between the Sabie and Crocodile rivers in the south and up the Lebombo hills. Sprints at close to 100km/h in bursts of no more than 30 seconds; must eat quickly before lions or hyenas home in. Rarely in thick bush, and never in the far north's mopane belt.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Mid-morning — hunts later than other cats

species.description: Small grey-brown antelope alone in the roadside grass; the male has thin straight horns, and both sexes show a dark stripe running down the muzzle. Bolts in a zig-zag rather than a straight line — 'duiker' means 'diver' in Afrikaans, from the diving weave through cover. Present throughout Kruger but easily overlooked because it's solitary, largely crepuscular, and never in the big herds people are scanning for. Browses on leaves rather than grass, and will take a fallen fruit or even a young bird if the chance turns up.
species.habitat: Bush and woodland with good cover

species.description: Africa's largest antelope — huge cattle-like body, a swinging dewlap under the throat, and spiral horns on both sexes. Uncommon in Kruger, with small herds mostly in the south around Malelane and Berg-en-Dal, plus scattered northern groups. Knees make a distinct clicking sound as the animal walks — audible at surprising distances, and thought to be an honest signal of size to would-be rivals. Bulls turn slate-blue with age. Can clear a 2.5m fence from a standstill, which is why boma-holding them is genuinely difficult.

Smallest African carnivore — russet-brown, roughly the size of a squirrel, standing sentry on top of a termite mound. Groups of 8 to 15 live inside disused termitaria, moving den every few weeks as the food thins around each one. Coordinated by constant high-pitched contact calls that stay running while they forage; a sudden silence means a threat overhead. Have a mutualism with Yellow-billed Hornbills that forage alongside them, sharing sentinel duty for a cut of the flushed insects. Common in mopane and mixed woodland throughout central Kruger.

Tiny rufous-grey mammal with a long trunk-like nose, darting between boulders on rocky koppies — usually you see only a blur across a rock ledge. One of Africa's 'Small Five'. Belongs to the ancient African group Afrotheria, meaning it's more closely related to elephants, aardvarks and hyraxes than to any true shrew or mouse. Not a rodent at all despite the name. Try the Lebombo koppies and rocky outcrops along the H1 near Satara at first light, when they emerge to sun briefly on the warm rocks.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Early morning on rocks, before the heat

species.description: Head above the acacia canopy, legs and neck out of proportion, chewing quietly at 5m up — usually the first giveaway from the car. Kruger holds several thousand, and they browse over 60 tree species, working around thorns with a 45cm blackish-purple tongue. Bulls stand with the tail hanging straight; cows tuck into a canopy to feed. Silent to human ears but produce infrasonic calls too low for us to hear. Give birth standing up — the calf drops nearly 2m to the ground, which apparently shocks its heart into action.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Any time — visible from a distance

species.description: Grey-brown with vertical white flank stripes and a fringed dewlap; bulls carry corkscrew horns that reach nearly 2m along the curl. Bounds across the road with tail flared white on the underside — that flash is the alarm signal, both to you and to other kudu. Wooded thickets throughout Kruger; commoner than the size suggests. Herds are usually cows and calves, with bulls separate except during the winter rut. Second-tallest antelope after eland. Powerlines and fences take a heavy toll on those horns each year.

Armour-plated body of overlapping brown scales, walking upright on the hind legs with the tail dragged behind — curls into a scaled ball when alarmed and even a lion cannot get through it. The world's most trafficked mammal, scales sold in Chinese medicine markets for fabricated ailments. A daytime road sighting in Kruger is a once-a-decade event and should be reported to any ranger straight away — SANParks tracks every individual seen. Feeds only on ants and termites, using a tongue longer than the animal's own body.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Night drives — a handful of sightings a year

population.note: Never counted — there is no survey that finds them. The honest answer is that nobody knows, and that guides work here for years without seeing one.

species.description: Massive dark shapes half-submerged in permanent pools — try Sunset Dam near Lower Sabie, the Olifants low-water bridge, or almost any bend of the Sabie River. Only eyes, ears and nostrils show by day; leaves the water at nightfall to graze up to 6km inland, following well-worn paths. Kills more people than any other African mammal by a wide margin. Never park between a hippo and its water, and never get out at a bridge where hippos have hauled out — a running hippo is faster than you think.

Low, stocky body, jet-black underneath with a bold silver-white saddle from crown to tail. Trots along at dawn and dusk almost oblivious to whatever's around, and will happily raid a beehive, dig out a puff adder, or steal a leopard's kill. Skin is loose and thick enough to survive porcupine quills and bee stings, and to twist inside if grabbed. Not seen every day in Kruger but common enough throughout — pay attention to jackal-sized dark shapes moving with real purpose in open country early or late.
species.habitat: Widespread; mostly nocturnal but active at dusk

species.description: Kruger's most abundant antelope, well over 100,000 head — russet-tan coat, black 'M' below the tail, and the male carries elegant lyre-shaped horns. Explosive high leaps when spooked, sometimes 3m up and 10m across, mostly to confuse a predator's timing. During the autumn rut the males roar like small lions and thunder around chasing females and rivals. Almost every predator in Kruger relies on them, which is why the population stays roughly the same year after year despite the losses.
species.habitat: Open woodland and the edges of riverine bush
species.bestTimeToSpot: Any time of day, year round

species.description: Small rock-antelope standing on tiptoes atop a boulder along the Lebombo hills or any rocky koppie — always in pairs, never solitary. Coat is hollow-tipped and springs back into place after a downpour, drying the animal quickly. Pairs mate for life and share a tiny territory; when one is feeding, the other is on watch, and they take it in turns. The whole weight sits on hoof-tips the diameter of a five-rand coin, giving grip on rock that no predator's paw can match.

Nocturnal — slender, cat-shaped, long ringed tail and large rosetted spots down the back and flanks. Comes into rest camps like Skukuza, Letaba and Olifants for scraps, and you'll see one along the fence line if you sit quietly with a torch after dinner. Not a cat at all despite the look — genets are viverrids, more closely related to civets and mongooses. Climbs like a squirrel, and hunts everything from insects to birds to small rodents. Common but almost never seen in daylight.
species.bestTimeToSpot: After dark in camp, or on night drives

species.description: Rosetted golden coat draped along a low branch, thick tail hanging — usually the shape of the tail against the sky is what gives one away. Most active dusk to dawn in riverine bush along the Sabie, Sand and Timbavati; around 1,000 in the park, and much commoner than sightings suggest. Solitary and territorial, but with overlapping ranges — a big male's territory can hold several females. Hauls kills into trees to keep them from lions and hyenas. Look up when scanning marulas and sausage trees.
species.habitat: Riverine bush, drainage lines and rocky ground
species.bestTimeToSpot: First and last light, on riverine roads

species.description: Never seen by day. Golden torch-eyes reflecting back at you from the trees around camp, then a 4m leap through the canopy on legs that fold like springs. Baby-like wailing calls after dark are diagnostic; once you know the call you'll hear them at almost every camp. Common in acacia and thorn woodland throughout Kruger. Wets its own hands and feet with urine to scent-mark trails, which means one bushbaby's night route is scented like a slug trail for others to follow.

Straw-coloured cats sprawled in shade, or a pride crossing at first light. Distant roaring carries 8km before dawn and is one of the sounds every Kruger visitor remembers. Around 1,600 in the park; best odds are the central plains around Satara and along the Sabie between Skukuza and Lower Sabie. Prides average 4-6 adult females with cubs, plus a coalition of one to four related males. Cubs are killed by any new male taking over the pride — the hard fact of pride succession.
species.habitat: Open woodland and grassland near prey concentrations

species.description: Small grey-fawn antelope on rocky slopes — short forward-curving horns on the male, a distinctive black scent-gland patch below the ear. Very few in Kruger; try the ridges above Berg-en-Dal in the south. Sharp whistle when startled, then bounds away with a tail-flash. Grazes short grass on hillsides that the bigger antelope cannot be bothered with. Kruger sits at the eastern edge of the species' range, which is why they're localised here — the stronghold is the Drakensberg and further west.

Rusty-slate males with narrow vertical white flank-stripes and lyre-tipped horns; females look like a different species entirely — bright chestnut, unhorned, boldly striped. Dense riverine bush in the north — Letaba camp is the reliable spot, and the boardwalks put you within metres of tame ones. A mixed herd of ten nyala can look like two species until you realise. The largest bulls carry a spinal crest of raised hair from head to rump, which stands up in threat display.

Black-and-white striped horses in mixed herds with wildebeest — no two individuals share a stripe pattern, and foals recognise their mother by hers within days of birth. Loud yelping bark when alarmed, quite unlike a horse's neigh. Common on the central plains from Satara to Lower Sabie. A stallion holds a harem of two to six mares plus their foals for several years at a time. What the stripes are actually for is still debated — thermoregulation and biting-fly deterrence are the leading theories.

Big, red-tan antelope with a striking black-and-white face-mask and long scimitar horns swept back over the shoulders — both sexes carry the horns. Fewer than 100 left in Kruger; try the far north around Shingwedzi and Mopani. Second-largest African antelope after eland. Very territorial and aggressive when cornered — the horns have killed pursuing lions. Herds are small and highly sensitive to disturbance, which is one of the reasons the Kruger population never recovered from the 1980s crash.

Bulls jet-black with a clean white belly, white face-mask and long scimitar horns swept back over the shoulders; cows and calves chestnut-brown. Small herds around Pretoriuskop and the western mopaneveld near Phalaborwa. Around 500 in the park — uncommon and localised. Fights between bulls involve dropping to the knees and clashing those horns, and they will genuinely kill each other. Considered by many old-guard hunters the most handsome antelope in Africa, which is a subjective claim but explains the trophy-room popularity.

Bounding at speed across the road in headlight beams, long black-tipped ears laid flat and the white belly flashing on each leap. Common everywhere in Kruger but crepuscular — dawn, dusk and night drives are the realistic chances. Sits absolutely still in the grass until you nearly stand on it, then breaks in a big zig-zag that would exhaust a serval. Doesn't dig a burrow; rests in a 'form' — a shallow scrape under a bush — even in heavy rain.

Long-legged spotted cat with huge upright ears, roughly Labrador-height at the shoulder — much taller than a caracal, and quite unlike a small leopard on the ground. Very rare from a car; try wet grasslands around Nsemani Dam and the roads near Satara at first light. Leaps to pounce on rodents through long grass by ear alone, sometimes vertically 2m before dropping onto the target. Needs grass tall enough to hide the body but let the ears work — the ears do the hunting.
species.habitat: Tall grass and reedbeds near water
species.bestTimeToSpot: Dawn and dusk in marshy areas

species.description: Small rufous-brown antelope speckled with white hairs on the back, giving the coat a grizzled look; the rump appears hunched. Only in dense bush in the north — Shingwedzi and Punda Maria are the best chances. Male has tiny straight horns; female none. Solitary and largely nocturnal, which is why almost every sighting is at dusk. Distinguish from the very similar Cape Grysbok by range — Cape Grysbok doesn't reach Kruger at all. Feeds on leaves and fallen fruit near the ground.

Rich rust-brown, long body low to the ground, tail held horizontally with a distinctive black tip flicked upright when running. Solitary — quite unlike the sociable Banded and Dwarf Mongooses. Bolts across the road with the unmistakable straight-out tail-flick, which is the giveaway even when you barely glimpse the animal. Common in mixed woodland throughout Kruger, and often around camp gardens. Takes small snakes, lizards, rodents and insects, and will occasionally raid a bird's nest at ground level.

Sandy-fawn antelope in tall reeds and grass near water; males have short forward-curving horns and a dark facial stripe. Small population in Kruger, mostly around Mopani and Shingwedzi where reedbeds and floodplain fringe survive. High-pitched whistle when alarmed, then a bounding retreat with a distinctive rocking-horse gait. Sits tight in tall grass until you're almost on top of it, then breaks with the whistle — surprises many first-time visitors. Grazes at night, rests hidden in dense cover by day.
species.habitat: Tall grass and reedbeds near water
species.bestTimeToSpot: Dawn and dusk in wetland areas

species.description: Barrel body, sloped back, dark spots on tan flanks, head lowered as it trots. Around 2,000 in Kruger — commoner than lion, and their whooping calls carry through the night. Clans of 20-plus around den sites, often under road culverts, and cubs come out to play at dusk if you sit quietly. Females are larger than males and rank higher; a hyena clan is a matriarchy. Take carcasses off lions when the numbers tip — a clan of fifteen can drive four lionesses off a kill.
species.habitat: Widespread; dens in culverts and drainage lines
species.bestTimeToSpot: Just after gate opening or before closing

species.description: Small rusty antelope, upright ears out of proportion to the tiny body, no belly stripe. Male has straight vertical horns; female has none. Common in open country throughout the park; often the antelope you see standing alone by the roadside. Bolts a short distance then freezes and looks back — a habit that has killed a great many of them, since a cheetah takes the second chance every time. Territorial pairs share a tiny range but sleep separately. Buries its dung to reduce scent.

Tiniest antelope in Kruger — reddish-brown, back speckled with white hairs, tail whipping side to side when moving. Restricted to the Pafuri sand forest in the far north; if you're anywhere else in Kruger, it isn't one. Strictly nocturnal and near-invisible in leaf-litter camouflage; a daytime sighting is genuinely exceptional. Adults weigh around 5kg — smaller than a big scrub hare. Feeds on fallen leaves and fruit under dense canopy, moving in the very dim understorey light before dawn and after dusk.
species.habitat: Dense sand forest and thicket in the far north

species.description: Larger than the lesser bushbaby, silver-grey with a bushy tail longer than the body. The piercing 'crying baby' scream at night around northern camps — Letaba, Punda Maria — is the diagnostic sound. Torch-eyes reflect a deep amber, not the lesser's gold. Common in tall riverine woodland along the Luvuvhu and Limpopo. Moves more slowly and heavily than the lesser bushbaby, climbing rather than leaping between branches. Wets its own hands and feet with urine to scent-mark routes across the canopy.
species.habitat: Riverine forest, especially in the north

species.description: Small grey-brown squirrel flicking a bushy tail on an acacia branch, chattering an alarm at anything larger than itself — often the first thing you hear at camp. All over the park in mixed woodland, and the loud 'chuk-chuk' scolding is a reliable predator-warning that other animals attend to. Nests in tree hollows in small family groups. Called the 'bushveld sentinel' for good reason — a persistent tree squirrel alarm above your head usually means something the size of a leopard is nearby.

Dark chestnut with a sloping back, and glossy purple-blue patches on the thigh and shoulder that catch the light — a good diagnostic when the head is hidden. Africa's fastest antelope, clocked at over 80km/h in level pursuit. Around 200 in the park, mostly the northern basalt plains near Mopani. Often standing high on a termite mound to scan for predators. Bulls mark territory with the pre-orbital gland pressed against grass stems, which is why you sometimes see one apparently kissing the ground.

Silver-grey coat, black face and white brow; males show an unmistakable turquoise-blue scrotum that a whole generation of biologists has written papers about. Troops of 20-30 around picnic sites and camps will grab food from a car window if you leave one open. Common throughout the park. Have distinct alarm calls for different predators — one for leopard, one for eagle, one for snake — and the troop responds differently to each. Never feed them; a fed vervet becomes a stealing vervet, and stealing vervets get shot.

Grey pig with wart-like facial pads and a tail held straight up like an antenna when trotting off — never mistake the tail flag. Often kneels on padded wrists to feed on grass roots. Sleeps in disused aardvark burrows, reversing in so the head and tusks face the entrance. Common in open country everywhere in Kruger. Only pig in daylight in open savanna, which makes a daytime pig almost certainly this. The upper tusks curl impressively but do very little damage; the lower ones do all the cutting.
species.habitat: Open grassland and around rest camps

species.description: Shaggy grey-brown coat with a bright white 'toilet-seat' ring encircling the rump — you cannot miss it, and no other antelope carries anything like it. Bulls carry heavy, ridged, forward-curving horns; cows are hornless. Always within a kilometre of permanent water, especially along the Letaba, Olifants and Sabie. The oily coat has a strong musky smell, long said to put predators off — lions take them regularly all the same. Takes to water when pursued, and can almost fully submerge in a pool.
species.habitat: Riverine grassland within a few kilometres of water

species.description: Wide square lip and a heavy shoulder hump for grazing, calf usually walking ahead of the mother. Numbers collapsed under poaching — around 2,000 left in the park, down from over 10,000 in 2010. Distinguish from Black Rhino by the square lip, larger size, and open-country grazing rather than bush-browsing. The 'white' is often explained as a mistranslation of the Dutch for wide, after that lip, but there is no evidence for it and the real origin is unknown — both rhinos are grey. Southern and central Kruger give the best odds; sit quietly at a dry-season waterhole.

population.note: SANParks stopped publishing rhino numbers so that poachers cannot use them. What is public is the direction: sharply down.

species.description: Nocturnal, long-legged and dog-sized, with a striking bushy pure-white tail that lights up in a torch beam. Largest African mongoose. Trots along tar roads in headlight beams, especially in the central section — Satara and Olifants night drives give the realistic chance. Solitary, quite unlike the sociable smaller mongooses. Feeds mostly on insects and small rodents, and will follow a herd of buffalo to snap up disturbed dung beetles. Almost never seen by day, so give up on self-drive and book a night drive.

Snake-like neck held above the water with body submerged — nicknamed 'snakebird'. Straight dagger bill separates it from cormorants' hooked one. Dries wings spread on branches over dams and rivers throughout Kruger.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Midday, wings out on a dead branch

species.description: White head, chest and tail with chestnut belly and black wings, perched high over water. The far-carrying yodel — head thrown back — is the signature sound of African rivers. Any permanent water in Kruger.

Slim grey hornbill with a plain dark curved bill — no casque, no bright colours. Piercing 'pee-pee-pee' whistle with the head lifted; undulating flap-flap-glide flight. Common throughout wooded Kruger.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Morning, calling from a bare branch

species.description: Black above, white underparts heavily streaked black — much smaller and more contrasted than Martial Eagle. Hunts in pairs from cover, often taking guineafowl and francolin; ringing 'klu-klu-kluee' call. Widespread woodland resident.
Rufous body with bold black-and-white wings and a fanned crest that flares like a mohawk. Probes lawns and short grass with the down-curved bill; soft 'hoop-hoop-hoop' call. Common around all camps.

Chestnut waterbird walking on lily pads with impossibly long toes, pale blue frontal shield above the bill. Females lay the eggs then leave the male to raise the chicks. Try any lily-covered dam or pan.
All-dark stork with an obvious gap between the closed mandibles — the openbill. Feeds on aquatic snails and freshwater mussels, using the bill as a nutcracker. Often in flocks at wetlands after rain.

All-white waterbird with an unmistakable spatulate bill sweeping side to side through shallow water — red bill and legs. Not to be confused with Great Egret; check the bill shape. Try Sunset Dam and Nsemani.
Adults have a black body, chestnut back and tail so short the feet stick out behind in flight, and bright red face and legs. Rocks side to side as it flies — the 'acrobat'. Kruger stronghold.
species.habitat: Open savanna, hunting on the wing

species.description: Grey heron with a completely black cap and nape — Grey Heron has only a black eye-stripe. Often hunts far from water in dry grassland, taking rodents and lizards. Widespread in Kruger.
species.habitat: Open grassland, often nowhere near water

species.description: Bold pied plover — black, white and grey plumage; red eye, black legs. Metallic 'tink-tink-tink' alarm sounds like a blacksmith's hammer on anvil. Any dam or waterhole edge in the park.

Solid chocolate-brown eagle with a large staring yellow eye and unfeathered pale legs — Tawny Eagle has feathered legs. Perches high and motionless, then drops on a snake. Widespread but scattered in Kruger.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Midday, perched on a dead tree

species.description: Big skulking cuckoo-relative — chestnut back and wings, cream underparts, red eye. The 'water bottle' call: liquid bubbling descending scale, often before rain. Dense thickets and reedbeds park-wide.

Uniform blue-green iridescent starling with a striking bright orange eye — smaller than Burchell's Starling. Everywhere at camps, picnic sites and hides, hopping under tables for crumbs. Whistled multi-note song.
species.bestTimeToSpot: All day, on the table next to you

species.description: Larger and paler-bodied than the common White-backed Vulture, with a honey-coloured eye. Occasional in Kruger, mostly wanderers from Blyde River escarpment cliffs where they breed. IUCN Vulnerable.
species.habitat: Ranges widely; breeds on cliffs elsewhere
species.bestTimeToSpot: At a large carcass, among White-backed Vultures

species.description: World's largest bird — flightless, 2m+ tall; males black-and-white, females plain brown. Very few in Kruger, mostly the far south around Malelane and Berg-en-Dal. Runs at 70km/h and kicks forward with a lethal claw.
species.habitat: Open short grassland and sparse savanna

species.description: Black cap encircled by a bright white ring — the 'crown'. Long red legs, mostly on dry short grassland — Blacksmith Lapwing prefers water edges. Loud 'kreep' alarm running around your car.
species.habitat: Short grass and recently burnt veld

species.description: Big fawn-brown goose with dark chestnut eye-patches — nothing else in Kruger looks like it. Loud honking pairs are aggressive around water. On every pan and dam in the park; often on camp lawns.
species.bestTimeToSpot: All day, at the water's edge

species.description: Plain pale-blue head, breast and belly with a chestnut back — no lilac breast, no long tail streamers, unlike Lilac-breasted Roller. Palearctic summer migrant, November to April. Often on roadside dead branches.
species.bestTimeToSpot: November to March only; a summer visitor

species.description: Glossy black bird with a distinctive forked tail and a piercing red eye. Sits alone on an exposed perch and hawks insects. Famous for mimicking predator calls to scare other birds off their food.
species.bestTimeToSpot: All day, on a fence or dead branch

species.description: Crow-sized kingfisher with a shaggy black-and-white crest and a massive black bill — biggest kingfisher in Africa. Male has chestnut breast; female has chestnut belly. Loud 'kack-kack-kack' along the Sabie and Olifants.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Early morning, low over the water

species.description: Rusty-red neck and head, slate back — like a Grey Heron scaled up, standing 1.5m tall. World's largest heron, solitary and motionless in shallows for tigerfish and catfish. Try Sunset Dam and Olifants.
species.habitat: Quiet backwaters of the big rivers and dams
species.bestTimeToSpot: Early morning, motionless at the water edge

species.description: Tall, all-white heron with a yellow bill and black legs — Little Egret has a black bill and yellow feet. Distinct kink in the neck when hunting. Common at pans and river edges throughout Kruger.
All-grey turaco with a tall backswept crest — a Kruger silhouette. Nasal drawled 'g'waaay' from the treetops, warning game of predators. Common in acacia and mopane throughout the park.
species.bestTimeToSpot: All day, complaining from the top of a tree

species.description: Grey heron with a thin black stripe from the eye to a nape crest — Black-headed Heron has a solid black cap. Yellow bill; stands motionless in water, hunting fish, frogs and rats. Widespread.
Dull bronze-grey ibis with a curved dark bill and a bright iridescent wing patch. The alarming 'haa-haa-haa-de-daaa!' shout at dawn is unmistakable — the sound of camp mornings across Kruger.

Uniform brown wading bird with an anvil-shaped 'hammer' head — the crest and heavy bill in perfect balance. Builds a massive stick nest above water, over 1m across, sometimes weighing 50kg. Widespread in Kruger wetlands.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Late afternoon, hunting frogs in shallow water

species.description: Grey polka-dot body, bald blue-and-red head with a horny helmet-casque on top. Flocks scuttling across the road in front of the car, cackling in alarm. Common everywhere in Kruger.

Small dark-brown vulture with a bare pinkish face and a fine slender bill for picking scraps — much smaller than Kruger's other vultures. IUCN Critically Endangered. Often first to arrive at a small carcass.
species.bestTimeToSpot: At a kill, on the outside of the crowd

species.description: Massive grey bustard with a crested head, walking sedately through open grassland. World's heaviest flying bird — males can reach 18kg per Guinness World Records. Try the central plains between Satara and Orpen.
Africa's largest vulture — massive black body, bare pink head with hanging skin folds ('lappets'). Rips through hides other vultures cannot. IUCN Endangered — one of Kruger's 'Big Six'.
species.habitat: Open savanna; nests in flat-topped trees

species.description: Turquoise, lilac, olive and blue — the lilac throat and breast plus long tail streamers separate it from European Roller. Sits high on dead branches, dropping on grasshoppers. Perhaps Kruger's most photographed bird.
species.habitat: Open woodland, perched on dead branches and posts

species.description: Smallest African bee-eater — bright green above, yellow throat with black gorget, cinnamon-buff belly. In pairs and small groups on low perches near water. Common throughout Kruger year-round.

Long black shrike — extremely long tapered tail, white shoulders and rump. Family parties of 4-8 perch prominently in trees; loud harsh 'skarrr-eee' whistled duet. Common in open acacia country, especially around Satara.

Tiny electric-blue kingfisher with a red bill and orange belly, crown barred black-and-blue. Sits low over water on reeds — Pygmy Kingfisher perches away from water. Any reed-fringed pan; try Lake Panic hide.
species.habitat: Reeded edges of dams and slow rivers
species.bestTimeToSpot: Morning, on a low reed at the water line

species.description: Massive stork with a bare pink head, dangling pink throat pouch and enormous straight bill. Stands stooped at carcasses beside vultures. Wingspan often over 2.5m — among the largest of any land bird.
species.habitat: Carcasses, rubbish pits and drying pans
species.bestTimeToSpot: Midday, at a kill or soaring on the thermals

species.description: Africa's largest eagle — dark brown head, white underparts speckled black, feathered legs, wingspan over 2m. Takes prey up to the size of a small antelope. IUCN Endangered — one of Kruger's 'Big Six'.
species.habitat: Open savanna; perches on tall dead trees

species.description: Massive rufous-orange owl, no ear tufts, black eyes — one of the biggest owls in Africa. Roosts in dense riverine trees along the Luvuvhu River in Pafuri, Kruger's only regular spot. One of the 'Big Six'.
species.habitat: Tall riverine forest along the Luvuvhu

species.description: Black-and-white kingfisher hovering on rapid wingbeats over water before dropping bill-first — the only Kruger kingfisher that hovers repeatedly. Rattling call. Any river, dam or pan in the park.
species.bestTimeToSpot: All day, hovering over open water

species.description: Purple crest, iridescent green head, red eye-ring. Brilliant scarlet primary flight feathers flash open in slow flight — the pigment is made from copper. Northern riverine forest, especially Pafuri and Punda Maria.
Big black weaver, males with a heavy blood-red bill and small white wing patch. Colonial haystack nests — messy piles of thorn twigs — dominate camp thorn trees. Common at Satara and Olifants.
species.habitat: Open woodland, usually near large trees and camps
species.bestTimeToSpot: All day, around camps and picnic sites

species.description: Brown bird clinging to giraffe, buffalo and antelope, red bill with a bright yellow eye-ring — Yellow-billed Oxpecker has a red-and-yellow bill. Hissing calls as it grooms ticks off its host.
species.habitat: On the backs of large mammals
species.bestTimeToSpot: Any time you find a buffalo herd

species.description: Small pale-brown weaver, red bill, breeding male with variable pink or buff face-mask. Forms clouds of thousands — the world's most abundant wild bird species. Best around Satara and dry-season waterholes.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Late afternoon, coming to drink in thousands

species.description: Huge black-and-white stork with the diagnostic tricoloured bill: red, with a black band and a yellow 'saddle' at the base. Male has dark eye, female yellow. One of the 'Big Six'; around 20 breeding pairs in Kruger.

Grey eagle-like head on ridiculously long pale legs — walks 20-30km a day hunting snakes. Long central tail feathers, black quills fanned behind the head; IUCN Endangered. Central grasslands around Satara.
species.habitat: Open grassland and lightly wooded savanna
species.bestTimeToSpot: Walking open ground in the morning

species.description: All carmine-red body with a turquoise crown and rump. Rides on kori bustards and even ostriches to catch flushed insects. Intra-African migrant, arriving in Kruger around September and departing March.
species.bestTimeToSpot: September to March only; a summer visitor

species.description: Turkey-sized black bird walking through grass; adult has bright red face and throat — female shows a dab of purple-blue on the throat. World's largest hornbill; IUCN Vulnerable (Endangered in South Africa). Booming dawn call carries 3km.

Breeding male has bright yellow body with a black face-mask that stops at the throat, and a red eye — Village Weaver has a black-and-yellow back and darker mask. Weaves round nests hanging from thorn trees.
species.habitat: Camps, reedbeds, anywhere with a thorn tree
species.bestTimeToSpot: Spring and summer, weaving over water

species.description: Slim red bill (the whole bill red, not yellow), pale head, spotted black-and-white back — the red bill is the diagnostic against Southern Yellow-billed Hornbill. Common in acacia woodland throughout Kruger.
species.bestTimeToSpot: All day, low down beside the road

species.description: Bright yellow banana-shaped bill on a hornbill with a spotted black-and-white back and pale head — nicknamed 'flying banana'. Bounces along beside cars begging at picnic sites. Common everywhere in Kruger.
species.bestTimeToSpot: All day, usually at eye level beside the road

species.description: Variable pale-fawn to dark brown eagle, feathered legs, gape reaching under the eye — Brown Snake Eagle has bare pale legs and a big yellow eye. Common perched eagle in open Kruger country.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Morning, soaring or on a kill

species.description: Small brown plover with a striking double black chest-band, white forehead and red eye-ring. Runs a few steps and stops on gravel edges of dams and rivers. Any low-water bridge in Kruger.
species.habitat: Muddy edges of dams and rivers
species.bestTimeToSpot: All day, at the water line

species.description: Africa's largest owl — pale grey plumage, salmon-pink eyelids visible when it blinks — a diagnostic mark by torchlight. Deep grunting 'hunh-hunh' at night. Widespread but scattered throughout Kruger.
species.habitat: Large trees along rivers and drainage lines
species.bestTimeToSpot: Dusk, or roosting by day if you know the tree

species.description: Grey-brown wader with a big yellow eye and pale grey wing-bar — Spotted Thick-knee has spotted wings and prefers dry ground. Always near water; trilling whistles at dusk. Try Sabie and Olifants sandbanks.

Pale golden-buff bird with an unmistakable heart-shaped white face — no ear tufts. Silent flight; blood-curdling screech at night. Roosts in disused buildings; check camp workshops and thatched roofs.
species.bestTimeToSpot: After dark, low along the road edge

species.description: Most abundant vulture in Kruger — dark brown body with a bright white lower back visible in flight (Cape Vulture is much paler overall). Cluster on carcasses in noisy squabbles. IUCN Critically Endangered.
species.habitat: Open woodland; nests in tall trees
species.bestTimeToSpot: Late morning, circling or at a carcass

species.description: White forehead, black eye-mask, brilliant red throat, buff belly — Little Bee-eater has a yellow throat. Colonial nester in vertical riverbanks; try Olifants and Letaba cuttings. Resident year-round in Kruger.

The only Kruger vulture with a clean white head and a pink-orange bill; black-and-white body. Often first at a carcass — hunts as well as scavenges. IUCN Critically Endangered; few pairs left in Kruger.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Late morning, first at a fresh carcass

species.description: Turquoise-and-blue kingfisher with a red upper bill and black lower — bright blue tail in flight. Piercing trilling call all day. Intra-African migrant, arriving mid-November and departing mid-March — the sound of Kruger summers.
species.bestTimeToSpot: November to March, calling from a bare branch

species.description: Glossy black stork with a fluffy white neck and belly — the 'wool' is diagnostic. Slow deliberate walk through wet ground and along rivers. Widespread but scattered in Kruger; often solitary.
White stork with a pink wash on the wings, red face and a slightly down-curved yellow bill. Wades in shallows sweeping the open bill from side to side. Try Sunset Dam and Lake Panic hide.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Morning, in groups at the water

species.description: Slate-grey to olive rather than black — the inside of the mouth is jet-black, hence the name. Up to 3m and among the world's fastest snakes. Shelters in termite mounds and hollow trees. Untreated bites are almost always fatal.
species.habitat: Woodland, termite mounds and rocky ground
species.bestTimeToSpot: Warm mornings — observe from the vehicle only

species.description: Slim tree snake, males emerald green, females olive-brown, with an outsized eye. Draped motionless along a branch. Rear-fanged; venom is highly dangerous but slow-acting, and the snake is calm — bites are rare.

Domed shell blotched black on yellow — named after the cat. The largest tortoise in southern Africa and one of the 'Small Five'. Often ambling across the road; drive round it, never lift or move one. Easily lives 80 years.

Grey-brown with pink-and-black throat bands visible when hooded. Sprays venom over 2m into the eyes, aimed at anything moving. Common around camps at night. If it hoods up, back away — do not throw anything.

Log-shape at the water's edge — often only eyes and nostrils showing, or a whole 4m body on a sandbank at midday. Explosively fast into water. Common in every permanent river; Sabie and Olifants are the best.

Thick, sluggish body patterned in grey-brown chevrons, arrow-shaped head. Lies motionless on roads and paths — the reason it accounts for more African snake bites than any other. Never step off a road onto grass without looking.
species.habitat: Everywhere; often on warm roads at dusk
species.bestTimeToSpot: Late afternoon, on tar still holding the day’s heat

species.description: Africa's largest snake — up to 5m, patterned brown and cream, non-venomous. Kills by constriction and will take small antelope. Often crossing roads warmed by tar. Protected inside Kruger.
species.habitat: Riverine bush, rocky outcrops and dense cover

species.description: Big grey-black lizard up to 2m, forked tongue flicking, laterally flattened tail for swimming. Along rivers and dams — often at Sunset Dam. Swims well and climbs trees. Bite is nasty; keep clear.

Look for tiny funnel-shaped pits in soft sand under thatch and along paths in rest camps — the larva waits at the bottom. Drop a grain of sand in and the trap-jaws will flick. Adult resembles a small, dull dragonfly. One of Africa's 'Small Five'.
species.habitat: Fine dry sand under trees, out of the rain
species.bestTimeToSpot: Any picnic site — look down before you look up

species.description: Chunky black or dark-brown beetle, males with a curved horn on the head — one of Africa's 'Small Five'. Buzzes into camp lights at night, especially in summer. Sluggish and harmless; grip strength is astonishing for the size.
species.habitat: Woodland; larvae develop in rotting wood and dung
species.bestTimeToSpot: Summer nights, at camp lights after rain

species.description: Massive smooth-barked trunk with stubby branches like roots pointed at the sky — the 'upside-down tree'. Only in the far north, from Punda Maria up to Pafuri. Some individuals over 1,000 years old; hollow trunks store thousands of litres of water.
species.habitat: Hot, dry country north of the Olifants
species.bestTimeToSpot: North of Mopani, impossible to miss

species.description: Tan coat with darker shoulders, a sloping back and lyre-shaped horns bent tight — often standing atop a termite mound scanning the plain. Reintroduced to the far north around Punda Maria in the 1980s after local extinction; a sighting anywhere in Kruger is a genuine piece of luck. Herds move slowly through open savanna near watercourses. Bulls are very territorial and will hold the same low ridge for years. Distinguish from Red Hartebeest by the flatter horn shape and browner tone.
species.habitat: Open sandveld and grassy woodland in the far north
species.bestTimeToSpot: Early morning on the Nwambiya sandveld, and mostly luck

species.description: Bare red throat and face, blackish bill and legs — Natal Spurfowl has an orange bill and no red throat. Male perches on a termite mound at dawn to give a rasping crow. Common in open bushveld.
species.habitat: Grassland, old lands and roadside verges
species.bestTimeToSpot: First hour of light, on the road edge

species.description: Mottled brown spurfowl with orange-red legs and bill — no bare red throat, unlike Swainson's Spurfowl. Grating rattle-call at dusk. Common in riverine bush and camps south of the Olifants River.
species.habitat: Thicket, riverine bush and rest camps

species.description: Small francolin with a dark cap, bold white eyebrow and short tail held cocked up like a bantam. Grating 'beer-and-cognac' duet at dawn. Common in mixed woodland — often on camp lawns.
Small lapwing with a plain brown body and only a small white forehead patch — much drabber than Blacksmith or Crowned. Very localised in Kruger — the north around Punda Maria on burnt grasslands.
species.habitat: Burnt grassland and bare short-grass plains

species.description: Jet-black crow with a clean white breast and collar — House Crow has grey shoulders. Deep 'kraw'; scavenges around gates, camps and roadkill. Widespread throughout Kruger.

Slender bustard with a very thin snake-like neck — nothing like the heavy Kori. Male has black belly stripe and gives a strange 'pop-and-whistle' display call with head thrown back. Open bushveld in the north.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Summer mornings, males calling from a rise

species.description: Small brown bustard with a raised red crest visible only in display. Male's dramatic aerial display: flies vertically 20m, folds wings, drops like a stone, pulls up at the last second. Common in dry bushveld.
Male has two chest bands — narrow white above, narrow black below — on a mottled brown body. Comes to drink at dusk in whistling flocks. Try Lake Panic hide and Sunset Dam at last light.
species.bestTimeToSpot: The last half hour before gate closing

species.description: Yellow wattles hanging from the face and yellow legs — separates it from other Kruger lapwings. Longer-legged and taller than Crowned or Blacksmith; loud 'kip-kip' alarm. Wet grasslands and floodplain fringes.
species.habitat: Damp grassland beside rivers and pans

species.description: White ibis with a bald black head and neck and a curved black bill; black wingtips visible in flight. The bird ancient Egyptians mummified in the millions. Wetlands and open ground throughout Kruger.
Chestnut-and-black duck with a clean white face — nothing else in Kruger looks like it. High three-note whistle in flight, often at night. Big rafts on pans and dams; try Sunset Dam and Lake Panic.
species.habitat: Pans, dams and quiet river edges

species.description: Small jet-black waterbird with a bright yellow bill, red eye and pink-red legs — no other Kruger rail looks like this. Walks on floating vegetation at pans and dam edges. Duet of croaks and clucks from the reeds.
species.habitat: Reeds and floating vegetation on quiet water
species.bestTimeToSpot: Early morning at a dam wall

species.description: Bare yellow face that flushes red when excited, long grey body, long tail with a single broad white bar. Double-jointed legs reach into weaver nests and tree holes for chicks. Also called 'Gymnogene'.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Mid-morning, working along a tree line

species.description: Small black cormorant with a hooked bill and a long tail — African Darter has a straight dagger bill. Perches drying wings after diving. Common on every dam and permanent river in Kruger.
Small white egret with a black bill, black legs and unmistakable bright yellow feet (the 'golden slippers') — Great Egret has a yellow bill. Actively chases fish in shallows with wings half-open.
Small stocky white egret with a thick neck and short yellow bill — Little Egret is slim with a black bill. Follows buffalo and elephant to snap up flushed insects. Common throughout the park.
species.bestTimeToSpot: All day, wherever the herds are

species.description: Grey-brown nightjar sitting lengthways on a branch or in the road at night. Song is unmistakable — 'Good-Lord-deliver-us' whistled repeatedly through the dark. Sit at any Kruger camp on a summer evening.
species.habitat: Woodland edges and the road itself
species.bestTimeToSpot: On a night drive, on the road surface

species.description: Tiny brown owlet with bold pearl-white spots on head and back, plus two big false 'eye' spots on the nape — decoy for predators approaching from behind. Ascending piped whistles even by day. Widespread.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Late afternoon — often mobbed by small birds

species.description: Tiny grey owl with pointed ear tufts, patterned like bark — you'll walk past it on a tree trunk. Soft frog-like 'prrrup' repeated every few seconds through the night. Try Skukuza staff-quarters trees.
species.bestTimeToSpot: After dark, torch on the call

species.description: Big black-and-white hornbill with a huge grey casque on top of the bill and red face-skin. Nasal wailing 'wa-a-a' call from the treetops — sounds like a crying baby. Northern riverine forest only, especially Pafuri.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Morning, in the big trees along a river

species.description: White underparts, chestnut crown and dark blue back — Barn Swallow has a dark throat. Two extremely thin 'wire' tail streamers on the male; perches on bridge railings. Common along Kruger rivers year-round.

Deep steel-blue back, rusty throat, long forked tail with white spots. Palearctic summer migrant to Kruger from October to April — the swallows over your car came from Europe. Perches on wires along tar roads.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Summer afternoons, low over the road

species.description: Chestnut crown, back and rump; underparts heavily streaked black on white — the stripes are the diagnostic. Perches on wires; nests as a mud tunnel under bridges and camp eaves. Common park-wide.
Slim pale-brown swift with a long deeply forked tail — always seen near palm trees, especially the fronds where it nests. Never lands on the ground. Try camps with palms — Skukuza, Lower Sabie.
Bill yellow with a red tip, no eye-ring — Red-billed Oxpecker has an all-red bill with a yellow eye-ring. Pale rump patch; prefers buffalo and giraffe. Uncommon in Kruger, more likely in the north.
species.habitat: On buffalo and giraffe, mostly in the north
species.bestTimeToSpot: Any time — scan a buffalo herd

species.description: Small black bush-shrike with a red eye. Male puffs the white back feathers into a cotton-ball above the tail in display — that's the diagnostic; repeated 'chick-weeeu' whistle from the canopy. Common in wooded thickets.
Glossy jet-black tit with a bright white wing-edge panel. Family parties acrobatically search branches for insects, with sharp 'chick-a-dee' calls. Common in mixed woodland throughout Kruger.

Bronze-green upperparts with bold white spots on the wings, cream underparts. Named for its ringing 'dee-dee-dee-derik' call, repeated all summer. Intra-African migrant, September to April; parasitises weavers.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Summer, calling from an exposed perch

species.description: Iridescent dark green body with a long white-barred tail and a curved red bill. Chattering, cackling parties of 6-12 rock back and forth in mock frenzy — the 'kakelaar' effect. Common in wooded camps.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Any time — you hear the party first

species.description: Scruffy grey-brown mousebird with a long tail and a shaggy crest — no red face patch, unlike Red-faced Mousebird. Bill dark above, pale below; untidy little parties bomb into fruiting trees. Common in camps.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Any time, in a fruiting bush

species.description: Grey mouse-like bird with a long tail, bright red face patch and red bill — Speckled Mousebird has a plain face and dark bill. Whistled 'zwee-wewitt' in fast direct flight. Common in fruiting trees.

Small green parrot with a dull brown head — no yellow shoulder patches, unlike Meyer's Parrot. Screeching flocks streaking overhead at treetop height, especially in mopane. Feeds on marula and other fruits.
species.habitat: Woodland with big trees, near water

species.description: Brown head, brown back with black streaks, turquoise wings, red bill. Hunts insects and lizards from a low perch — not tied to water despite the name. Common in mixed woodland throughout Kruger.
species.habitat: Woodland and camp gardens, often away from water
species.bestTimeToSpot: Any time, on a low perch

species.description: Rusty-chestnut crown and back, turquoise-blue underparts, bright yellow throat with a black gorget — the most colourful bee-eater in Kruger. Palearctic summer migrant, October to April, calling 'krruup' as flocks pass overhead.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Summer, hawking high over open ground

species.description: Yellow-green pigeon clambering parrot-style through fig-tree branches — often only the shaking leaves give it away. Red base to the bill, yellow legs; guttural chuckles from the canopy. Try riverine figs at Skukuza or Letaba.

Larger and darker than Cape Turtle Dove, with a bare red eye-ring on a red eye. Slow six-note call rendered as 'I-AM-a red-eyed dove'. Common in wooded areas throughout Kruger, particularly around camps.
Pale grey-fawn dove with a thin black half-collar and a black eye. Three-note call rendered locally as 'work HARD-er, work HARD-er'. Also known as the Ring-necked Dove — Kruger's most common dove.
Small pinkish-brown dove with a black-speckled brown throat patch — no neck ring, unlike Cape Turtle Dove. Bouncing bubbling laugh as its call. Common in every camp, walking on paved paths.
species.habitat: Camps, roadsides and dry open ground

species.description: Grey-and-white shrike with a wispy white crest, yellow-fleshed eye-wattle and a bright yellow eye. Chattering parties of 6-10 move through the canopy together, with whistled 'weep' contact calls. Common in mixed woodland.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Morning, when the party comes past

species.description: Bright scarlet face and throat with a thick black collar — nothing else in Kruger looks like this. Duetting pair sings 'too-poodly, too-poodly' in perfect sync. Common around camps and picnic sites.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Morning, duetting from a bare branch

species.description: Yellow-and-red spotty little tank with a shaggy black crest and speckled black wings. Continuous alarm-clock trill — 'trrrrrrrrrrr' — is the diagnostic sound. Common in camp gardens throughout Kruger.

Big-billed hunter — grey head, olive back, yellow underparts washed orange on the chest. Skulks in thick canopy; the 'ghost bird' whistle is a mournful drawn-out 'oooooop'. Wooded thickets throughout Kruger.
Bright golden-yellow body with a jet-black head and a coral-pink bill. Liquid 'pooo-lyow' whistle from the canopy — often heard before seen. Common in tall trees around camps.

Brown babbler with distinctive white arrow-shaped streaks across the throat and chest, and a pale yellow eye. Loud collective chattering as parties of 6-12 crash through camp bush. Common around Skukuza and Letaba.
Brown bulbul with a black-brown cap and a bright yellow vent — the yellow rump patch under the tail is the giveaway. Loud liquid 'sweet-potato' morning song from every camp fence. Common park-wide.

White breast heavily spotted with black — unlike Kurrichane Thrush's plain buff underparts. Upright stance on the ground with tail flicked down; whistled song. Common on open grassy ground and camp lawns.

Orange bill, plain orange-buff flanks, black malar stripe on the throat — no bold black spotting like Groundscraper Thrush. Hops on shaded lawns and camp gardens; mellow song at first light. Common park-wide.

Small warbler that looks tailless — barely any tail at all — with a long down-curved bill. Grey above, buff below, creeping along branches to glean insects. Common in acacia woodland throughout Kruger.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Morning, in a mixed bird party

species.description: Small warbler, grey head, olive back, bright yellow breast — no black throat bar (Bar-throated Apalis has one). Long fine tail flicked side to side. Common in mixed woodland canopies throughout Kruger.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Morning, high in a thorn tree

species.description: Rufous back and tail, steel-blue head; the breeding male grows two central tail feathers longer than his body. Zigzagging sallies from riverine bush. Common October to April, scarcer in winter.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Summer mornings, low in the shade

species.description: Big violet-blue glossy starling with a long tail, walking on the ground — clearly larger and longer-tailed than Cape Glossy Starling. Gruff chirping calls. Try mopane country in the north around Punda Maria.
species.bestTimeToSpot: All day, often on the ground

species.description: Slate-grey back, orange underparts, long orange tail, and a bold white eyebrow — the eyebrow is diagnostic against other robin-chats. Melodic dawn song with mimicry. Common in riverine bush around Skukuza and Letaba.
Bold black-and-white wagtail — much more contrasted than the Cape Wagtail. Runs along rocks at rivers and dams, tail pumping constantly; sings a musical warble at dawn. Try low-water bridges.
species.habitat: River edges, rocks and low-water crossings
species.bestTimeToSpot: Any time, at a river crossing

species.description: Breeding male black with a white wing-panel and a yellow shoulder — much smaller than Long-tailed Widowbird. Non-breeding male and female streaky brown. In tall grass and reedbeds throughout Kruger.

Breeding male yellow, black head extending over the whole face and throat, back spotted black-and-yellow — Southern Masked Weaver has a plain yellow back and smaller mask. Noisy colonies in riverine trees.
species.habitat: Trees over water, camps and rivers

species.description: Breeding male is startling scarlet-orange with a black face and belly, fluffing out in display over reedbeds. Non-breeding male and female drab streaky brown. Colonies in reed-fringed pans, widespread wherever wet vegetation persists.
species.habitat: Reedbeds and rank grass near water

species.description: Male has an iridescent metallic-green head and chest above a clean white belly, thin curved bill. Female drab olive with white belly. Common in flowering aloes and camp gardens throughout Kruger.

Male matt-black with a metallic green crown and throat and a brilliant scarlet chest — nothing else looks like it. Female drab olive-brown speckled below. Common in flowering aloes and camp gardens throughout Kruger.

Small yellow-and-olive canary — bright yellow underparts and eyebrow, black malar stripe curving down from the bill. Melodious warbling song from thorn trees. Common in mixed woodland and camp gardens.
Plain grey head (no black face-mask like House Sparrow), chestnut back, one thin white wing-bar. Common at picnic sites and camp lawns, hopping under tables. Whistled 'chirrup-chirrup' call.
Sky-blue face, breast and belly with fawn back — a small seedeater flitting under acacias, often at camp bird tables. High squeaky call. Common everywhere in mixed woodland.

Striped black-and-white head, chestnut back, bright yellow underparts with an orange-yellow breast. Small seedeater, singly or in pairs on the ground under trees; sweet warbling song. Widespread in Kruger mixed woodland.

Slender, upright fawn antelope with a black scent-gland patch below the ear and thin straight horns on the male. Very rare in Kruger — only a handful survive, mostly on the grasslands around Pretoriuskop in the south-west. Bounces off with stiff-legged 'stotting' when flushed, showing the black tail-tip. Prefers short grass with taller cover nearby, a habitat that's shrunk everywhere in South Africa. If you see one, note the exact location and mention it at camp reception — sightings feed a conservation register.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Early morning on the Pretoriuskop grasslands, and mostly luck

species.description: Sleek dark-brown swimmer with a pale creamy throat, usually in family groups of two to five along the Sabie, Olifants and Letaba rivers. Uses hand-like forepaws rather than teeth to grab crabs and freshwater mussels from under rocks — the 'clawless' name refers to the front paws only, which have fingers rather than claws. Almost always seen from a bridge or riverbank at first light, before boats and heat move them into deeper cover. Emerges onto rocks to eat, leaving broken shells behind.
species.bestTimeToSpot: First light at a low-water crossing, sitting very still

species.description: Male has an emerald-green back with a brilliant scarlet belly; female has a brown face and throat. Sits still on a horizontal branch, always facing away, so you see only the green. Try Pafuri riverine forest.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Summer mornings in the Luvuvhu forest, listening for a low hoot

species.description: Dark grey with a black face and pale throat — distinct from the vervet's silvery grey and darker face-mask. Found only in the tall riverine and sand forest of Pafuri and Punda Maria in the far north; you won't see them anywhere else in Kruger. Loud booming male call carries from the canopy at dawn, deeper than a vervet's call. Troops of 15-30 stay in the trees more than vervets do. Kruger holds the southernmost population of a subspecies that ranges up into East Africa.
species.habitat: Tall riverine forest, Pafuri and the Luvuvhu
species.bestTimeToSpot: Morning, high in the trees — listen for the branches

species.description: Flat olive-brown shell, long neck tucked sideways not backwards. Basking on logs and rocks in seasonal pans and mud pools. When a pan dries it buries into cracked mud and waits, sometimes years, for the next rains.
species.habitat: Seasonal pans, dams and slow water
species.bestTimeToSpot: After summer rain, walking between pans

species.description: Finely barred grey head and breast — the barring separates it from Pearl-spotted Owlet's spots and false 'eyes' on the nape. Rapid 'kroo-kroo-kroo' trill at dusk. Try mopane woodland in the north.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Dusk, along the Luvuvhu and Sabie rivers
